Clopen Sets

This scene is about sets both open and closed: clopen sets. The same set changes its fate with the space it lives in.

On the whole real line, only the empty set and the line itself qualify. A boundary always appears somewhere. But if the space splits into two separate pieces, one piece touches no boundary. That piece is both open and closed.

For example, take one of two far-apart 🏠 houses. In a world made of that house alone, it forms its own separate region. It is open, and it is closed.

A clopen in X  ⟺  A open in X and closed in XA \text{ clopen in } X \iff A \text{ open in } X \text{ and closed in } XA clopen in X⟺A open in X and closed in X
[0,1]=([0,1]∪[2,3])∩(−0.5,1.5)=([0,1]∪[2,3])∩[−0.5,1.5][0,1] = \bigl([0,1]\cup[2,3]\bigr) \cap (-0.5, 1.5) = \bigl([0,1]\cup[2,3]\bigr) \cap [-0.5, 1.5][0,1]=([0,1]∪[2,3])∩(−0.5,1.5)=([0,1]∪[2,3])∩[−0.5,1.5]

For the subspace X=[0,1]∪[2,3]⊆RX = [0,1] \cup [2,3] \subseteq \mathbb{R}X=[0,1]∪[2,3]⊆R and A=[0,1]A = [0,1]A=[0,1], prove completely that AAA is clopen in XXX but not open in R\mathbb{R}R.

[0,1]=X∩(−1/2, 3/2)=X∩[−1/2, 3/2][0,1] = X \cap (-1/2,\, 3/2) = X \cap [-1/2,\, 3/2][0,1]=X∩(−1/2,3/2)=X∩[−1/2,3/2]
Show proof

  1. Openness in XXX: check [0,1]=X∩(−1/2, 3/2)[0,1] = X \cap (-1/2,\, 3/2)[0,1]=X∩(−1/2,3/2).

    Since (−1/2, 3/2)(-1/2,\, 3/2)(−1/2,3/2) is open in R\mathbb{R}R, [0,1][0,1][0,1] is open in XXX.

  2. Closedness in XXX: the same argument gives [0,1]=X∩[−1/2, 3/2][0,1] = X \cap [-1/2,\, 3/2][0,1]=X∩[−1/2,3/2] (since [2,3]∩[−1/2, 3/2]=∅[2,3] \cap [-1/2,\, 3/2] = \emptyset[2,3]∩[−1/2,3/2]=∅).

    As [−1/2, 3/2][-1/2,\, 3/2][−1/2,3/2] is closed in R\mathbb{R}R, [0,1][0,1][0,1] is closed in XXX.

So the same set [0,1][0,1][0,1] is clopen in XXX while in R\mathbb{R}R it is merely closed, not open — clopenness is relative to the ambient space.

Let XXX be a topological space and A⊆XA \subseteq XA⊆X clopen.

Prove completely that if ∅≠A≠X\emptyset \ne A \ne X∅=A=X then XXX is disconnected.

X=A∪Ac,A∩Ac=∅,A, Ac≠∅ open in XX = A \cup A^c, \qquad A \cap A^c = \emptyset, \qquad A,\, A^c \ne \emptyset \text{ open in } XX=A∪Ac,A∩Ac=∅,A,Ac=∅ open in X
Show proof

  1. If AAA is clopen then so is its complement Ac=X∖AA^c = X \setminus AAc=X∖A: complementation swaps openness and closedness (AAA open makes AcA^cAc closed; AAA closed makes AcA^cAc open).

  2. Since ∅≠A≠X\emptyset \ne A \ne X∅=A=X, both AAA and AcA^cAc are nonempty.

    Moreover X=A∪AcX = A \cup A^cX=A∪Ac, A∩Ac=∅A \cap A^c = \emptysetA∩Ac=∅, and both are open in XXX — a separation of XXX.

    Hence XXX is disconnected.

  3. The converse holds too: if X=U∪VX = U \cup VX=U∪V is a separation then U=X∖VU = X \setminus VU=X∖V is also closed, hence clopen.

    So "a nontrivial clopen set exists" is equivalent to "disconnected".

    Problem 1 above is the special case X=RX = \mathbb{R}X=R — since R\mathbb{R}R is connected, no nontrivial clopen set can exist there.
